BEN-02.title: A binary replication label changes with precision alone, and one operator carries almost all of it
BEN-02.question: BEN-02 says replication is reported as a binary label that mixes estimand mismatch with random error. Holding the true trial-emulation discrepancy fixed, how much of the label is decided by precision rather than by the discrepancy, and which of the operators in use carries that sensitivity?
BEN-02.design: 16 structural scenarios crossing the true risk-difference discrepancy with trial and emulation precision, 10,000 replicates each, 480,000 benchmark pairs. Each replicate is one trial cohort and one emulation cohort with a binary outcome, scored by four agreement operators in current use. Truth is enumerated by exact summation over the covariate strata rather than by simulation, so the discrepancy each scenario carries is known to machine precision.
BEN-02.estimand: The probability that a pair-level agreement operator returns agreement, as a function of precision at a fixed true discrepancy, and the sensitivity S of that probability to precision alone
BEN-02.answer: For the operators tested, yes, and it is concentrated in one of them. The sensitivity S is the larger of the two operator-specific values at 0.4915, against a threshold of 0.10 declared before the run, with a 95 percent Monte Carlo interval of 0.4903 to 0.4931; the lower endpoint clears the threshold by roughly 538 Monte Carlo standard errors. Confidence-interval overlap supplies that value; direction agreement moves by 0.1244 over the same range. Two benchmark pairs carrying the same true discrepancy can therefore be labeled agreeing and disagreeing on the strength of how precisely each was estimated, and the operator most used to produce the label is the most exposed.
findings: The label moves with precision at fixed truth. Holding the true risk-difference discrepancy constant and varying only trial and emulation precision moves the probability of an agreement verdict by 0.49 on the interval-overlap operator, against a threshold of 0.10 set in the protocol before any result existed.

The exposure is not shared evenly. Direction agreement moves by 0.1244 over the same range, a quarter of the interval-overlap figure. An operator choice that is usually made for convenience decides most of the conflation.

It is not an estimation artifact. Coverage runs 0.944 to 0.956 against a nominal 0.95, maximum absolute bias is 0.00086, convergence is complete in every scenario, and the exact finite-cell summation used for truth agrees with itself to 2.2e-16. Nothing here is an estimator failing.
The bootstrap interval is narrow enough to matter. The Monte Carlo interval on S spans 0.0028, so the distance from the 0.10 threshold is not a Monte Carlo question.
BEN-02.not_answered: S is the maximum over the operators tested, so the result is an at-least-one-operator claim: it establishes that interval overlap is materially precision-sensitive and that direction agreement is less so, not that every binary replication label is. It holds for these two illustrative operators, these 16 fixed scenarios and these three nested precision levels. This is the pair-level component of BEN-02 and not the entry as a whole: it says nothing about between-pair heterogeneity across a benchmarking program, about calibration of a graded metric against a decision, or about the graded alternatives the entry's own audit established already exist, all three of which the design review named as out of scope and which are declared limitations rather than results. Outcomes are binary at a single horizon, so the behavior of these operators on a time-to-event scale is untouched.
BEN-02.peer_review: The design was reviewed before running and returned unsound with three fatal findings: it answered a neighboring question, its mechanism solved the eligibility parameter to produce the discrepancies it then measured, and its decision rule had an unreachable negative branch. All three were resolved in a revision pass before any code was written. The results were then reviewed in a fresh context that saw the protocol and the result files but not the study's own summary, and returned supported on the first round with one minor finding about scope, folded into the wording above.

CNF-01.title: A single cumulative-initiation number at the horizon does not determine the attenuation it is asked to explain
CNF-01.question: CNF-01 asks authors to publish the cumulative incidence of initiation in both arms so a reader can see how far the contrasted strategies stayed distinct, and to quantify by simulation how much attenuation a given convergence rate produces. Does that diagnostic actually recover the attenuation?
CNF-01.design: Discrete monthly time to 10 years, 4000 individuals per replicate, confounded baseline initiation, later initiation in the comparator arm, and a treatment that works. 24 scenarios crossing three convergence rates, two timing shapes tuned to the same cumulative initiation at the horizon, initiation that does or does not concentrate in high-risk patients, and two effect-persistence regimes. 1000 replicates each, 24,000 replicates in all. Truth enumerated from the mechanism at two million individuals per scenario rather than estimated from the replicates.
CNF-01.estimand: Risk difference at horizons of 1 to 10 years for assignment to initiate at baseline versus not, with later initiation left to run, against the always-treated versus never-treated contrast the comparator arm would have supported had it stayed untreated
CNF-01.answer: No. Within the simulated grid, comparator-arm cumulative initiation at 120 months does not uniquely determine attenuation: matched early and late initiation scenarios, whose reported diagnostic agrees to within 0.0005, differ in attenuation by 0.0528 to 0.2027. Nine of the twelve matched pairs exceed the 0.05 threshold declared before the run by at least three Monte Carlo standard errors, at 5 to 46 of them; the other three sit within 3 and are individually inconclusive, and all three are at the lowest convergence rate, where there is least attenuation to misattribute. A single cumulative-incidence value at the horizon is therefore insufficient for recovering attenuation in these scenarios. What the reported number cannot see is when the comparator arm initiated and who initiated.
findings: The insufficiency scales with convergence, which is the opposite of reassuring. At 20 percent cumulative initiation the matched difference is 0.053 to 0.070 and only one of four pairs is established; at 45 percent it is 0.116 to 0.145 at 18 to 27 Monte Carlo standard errors; at 70 percent it is 0.181 to 0.203 at 39 to 46. The diagnostic is least informative exactly where attenuation is largest.

Attenuation is large and grows with the horizon. Pooled across scenarios its median is 0.024 at one year and 0.245 at ten, with a maximum of 0.567. A treatment that genuinely works can lose more than half its sustained-strategy effect to convergence alone.

Who initiates matters as much as when. Concentrating initiation in high-risk patients raises attenuation from 0.476 to 0.567 at the highest convergence rate. The reported diagnostic, measured among observed non-initiators, stays at 0.700, while initiation under assignment to not initiating reaches 0.742: baseline confounding leaves lower-risk patients in the observed comparator arm, so the reported number understates the convergence of the assigned strategy.

Effect persistence is the factor that matters least. Transient and legacy regimes differ in attenuation by at most 0.034, at 24 months while the 12-month ramp is still under way, and by at most 0.014 at 120 months, against a spread across scenarios of 0.16 at one year and 0.50 at ten.

The estimators show small finite-sample bias rather than none. Coverage runs 0.934 to 0.970 against a nominal 0.95 and convergence is complete, but 14 of 288 cells carry bias beyond three Monte Carlo standard errors, to a maximum of 4.2. That does not touch the decisive comparison, which uses attenuation enumerated from the mechanism at two million individuals per scenario rather than estimated attenuation.
CNF-01.not_answered: The comparison holds the diagnostic fixed only at 120 months. At earlier horizons the early and late scenarios differ in observed cumulative initiation by as much as 0.269, so those contrasts are not comparisons at equal C(h) and cannot independently establish insufficiency there. The study establishes that C(120) alone is insufficient within this grid. It does not establish that reporting C is necessary, that the full initiation curve would be sufficient, or that a universal conversion from convergence to attenuation exists. The comparator arm converges upward and the treated arm never discontinues, so this is one direction of convergence only. There is no loss to follow-up and no competing event, both excluded so the attenuation is not confounded with a second mechanism. The scale is the risk difference throughout; a hazard ratio would mix this mechanism with non-collapsibility.
CNF-01.peer_review: Three rounds of results review, each in a fresh context that saw the catalog entry, the registered protocol and the result files but not the study's own summary. Round 1 returned uninformative with two fatal findings: the decisive quantity carried no Monte Carlo uncertainty, so its distance from the threshold could not be compared with its own error. Adding that uncertainty changed the finding, from twelve of twelve matched pairs clearing the threshold to nine. Round 2 returned three serious findings, one of which was an arithmetic error in the study's own reporting: bias was described as a share of the attenuation and computed against the risk difference, understating it by two orders of magnitude. Round 3 returned supported with three minor findings about claim strength, all folded into the wording above.

PRO-02.title: A recorded, effect-blind search over highly correlated protocols leaves naive intervals close to nominal on average, and undercovering when the candidates disagree
PRO-02.question: PRO-02 says inference conditions on a fixed target trial that was in fact selected after seeing the data. When the search is recorded and the selector is blind to the treatment effect, choosing among 4 or 16 candidate protocols by outcome counts or covariate-outcome associations, how much coverage do naive 95% intervals for the selected protocol lose, and what do Bonferroni correction and sample splitting cost?
PRO-02.design: 36 generated-data cells crossing cohort size (4000, 8000), expected pooled events at the anchor protocol (age at least 55, 36 months: 35, 70 or 140), library size (4 or 16 candidates over nested age thresholds and outcome horizons) and treatment effect (null, hazard ratio 0.75, age-modified), 2000 replicates each. Four selectors that never see the treatment effect: a workability rule on arm sizes and pooled event counts, two prognostic-association rules differing in how closely their fixed score tracks the outcome, and an outcome-blinded covariate-balance rule; an effect-seeking selector is the positive control. Hajek inverse probability weighted risk differences with a correctly specified propensity model. Truth by numerical integration to a Monte Carlo standard error of at most 0.0000166. A first run with the same design failed its registered calibration gate by chance and was recorded as inconclusive; this is the separately registered replication with a new seed and a gate that allows for Monte Carlo error across the 360 fixed-candidate evaluations.
PRO-02.estimand: Unconditional coverage of the naive 95% interval for the selected protocol's risk difference, as the deficit D = 0.95 minus coverage, globally (D_all) and outside the near-boundary event-count regime (D_nonboundary)
methods_compared: naive interval after workability, prognostic-association or outcome-blinded selection
naive interval after effect-seeking selection (positive control)
PRO-02.n_sim: 2000 per cell, 36 cells, 1,728,000 rows, 0 replicate errors
PRO-02.answer: Not materially, within this design. The global deficit D_all was 0.0015 (simultaneous 95% Monte Carlo interval -0.0001 to 0.0030) and D_nonboundary 0.0023 (0.0004 to 0.0042), both upper limits far below the registered 0.02 threshold; all 360 fixed-candidate evaluations passed the calibration gate. The nonboundary deficit is detectably above zero, but it is about a fifth of a percentage point. Averaged over replicates, a recorded, effect-blind choice among these protocols costs naive intervals almost nothing.
findings: The average hides a conditional failure. Naive noncoverage was 0.022 to 0.025 when the candidates' estimates spanned less than one standard error, 0.041 to 0.044 when they spanned one to two, and 0.082 to 0.083 when they spanned more than two. The spread of the candidate estimates predicts noncoverage with an AUC of 0.66 to 0.68, so a reader who sees a wide multiverse has reason to distrust the selected interval even though coverage is nominal on average.

The design can see a coverage loss when there is one. Selecting the protocol with the largest effect estimate, the registered positive control, lowered naive coverage to 0.922 on average under the null and to 0.894 to 0.928 across the 16-candidate cells, against 0.946 to 0.951 for the effect-blind selectors. Even deliberate effect seeking loses only two to five percentage points here, because the candidates are so highly correlated.

The libraries were nearly one protocol. Nested age thresholds and outcome horizons produce highly correlated candidates: the effective library size was 1.37 to 1.39 for 4 candidates and 1.76 to 1.85 for 16. Little is being searched over, which is why the average deficit is small. Libraries of less correlated protocols are untested.

Both remedies worked and both cost precision. Selected-protocol Bonferroni intervals covered 0.9915, overshooting nominal; sample splitting covered 0.947 and gave intervals a median 1.42 times as wide as the full-sample interval for the same candidate, close to the square root of two expected from halving the data.

The first run's gate failure was chance. It required every one of 360 coverage estimates to lie in [0.93, 0.97] and one came in at 0.9285, 0.26 Monte Carlo standard errors outside. The replication, drawn from a new seed under a gate registered before it ran, passed all 360, with coverage 0.929 to 0.961.
PRO-02.not_answered: The conclusion covers deterministic recorded searches over nested age thresholds and outcome horizons, libraries of 4 or 16 highly correlated candidates, treatment-effect-blind selectors, and correctly specified inverse probability weighting. It does not cover undocumented or sequential protocol development by an analyst who has seen results, other protocol components such as grace periods or treatment definitions, libraries of weakly correlated protocols, or misspecified weights. The replication's calibration gate controls false failure across 360 comparisons and in exchange would pass a candidate miscalibrated by less than about two percentage points.
PRO-02.peer_review: The design was reviewed and revised before any code was written. The first run's results were reviewed twice and the registered classification was held at uninformative because the calibration gate failed; the reviewer's recommendation, a separately registered replication with a gate that allows for Monte Carlo error, is what produced this result. The replication's own results have not yet been reviewed.
